guide.summary: Unit 4 covers markets where firms have price-setting power: monopoly (including natural monopoly and regulation), price discrimination, monopolistic competition, and oligopoly analyzed with game theory. The key skills are graphing a monopolist's MR, MC, ATC, and demand; finding profit, consumer surplus, and deadweight loss; and solving payoff matrices.

sections.heading: Monopoly
sections.body: A monopoly is a single seller of a product with no close substitutes, protected by barriers to entry (control of resources, patents, government licenses, economies of scale). The monopolist faces the downward-sloping market demand curve, so to sell more it must lower price on all units: MR lies below demand (for linear demand, MR has twice the slope). It produces where MR = MC and charges the price on the demand curve at that quantity. Because P > MC, output is below the allocatively efficient level, creating deadweight loss, and P > minimum ATC, so it isn't productively efficient. A monopolist always produces on the elastic portion of demand (where MR > 0). It can earn economic profit in the long run because of barriers to entry.

sections.heading: Natural monopoly and regulation
sections.body: A natural monopoly occurs when economies of scale are so large that one firm can supply the whole market at lower cost than several firms (utilities). Regulators may set the socially optimal price (P = MC), which is allocatively efficient but may cause losses requiring a subsidy (since ATC > MC when ATC is falling), or a fair-return price (P = ATC), which yields zero economic profit with some deadweight loss. A price ceiling on a monopolist set at the competitive level can increase output.

sections.heading: Price discrimination
sections.body: Price discrimination means charging different prices to different consumers for the same good, not based on cost differences. Requirements: market power, ability to separate customers by willingness to pay, and prevention of resale. Perfect (first-degree) price discrimination charges each customer their maximum willingness to pay: MR equals demand, output reaches the efficient level, there is no deadweight loss, and the firm captures all consumer surplus.

sections.heading: Monopolistic competition
sections.body: Many firms sell differentiated products with low barriers to entry (restaurants, clothing). Each faces a downward-sloping demand, sets MR = MC, and may earn short-run profits. Entry shifts each firm's demand left until it is tangent to ATC: zero economic profit in the long run, with P > MC (not allocatively efficient) and output below minimum ATC (excess capacity, not productively efficient). Firms use advertising and product differentiation.

sections.heading: Oligopoly and game theory
sections.body: An oligopoly has a few interdependent firms with high barriers to entry. Game theory models strategic interaction. A dominant strategy is best regardless of the other player's choice. A Nash equilibrium is an outcome where each player's strategy is a best response to the other's; no one can gain by changing alone. The prisoners' dilemma shows that individually rational choices can produce an outcome worse for both than cooperation. Collusion and cartels raise joint profits but are illegal in many countries and unstable because each member has an incentive to cheat. To solve a payoff matrix, compare each player's payoffs for each of the other's choices, then look for mutual best responses.

sections.heading: Worked example: monopoly
sections.body: A monopolist's marginal revenue curve lies below its demand curve because to sell another unit it must lower the price on all units. It produces where MR = MC and charges the price on the demand curve at that quantity. Compared with perfect competition, the monopolist produces less and charges more, creating deadweight loss. A natural monopoly, with economies of scale over the market's relevant output, may be regulated to charge a fair-return price (P = ATC) or a socially optimal price (P = MC), which may require a subsidy.

sections.heading: Oligopoly and game theory in practice
sections.body: In a payoff matrix, a dominant strategy is the best choice regardless of the other player's choice. A Nash equilibrium occurs when neither player can improve by changing strategy alone. The prisoner's dilemma shows why firms may fail to cooperate even when collusion would benefit both. Monopolistic competition has many firms selling differentiated products, earning zero economic profit in the long run with excess capacity.

keyTakeaways: Monopoly: MR < D; produce MR = MC; price from demand.
Monopoly creates DWL because P > MC.
Perfect price discrimination: MR = D, no DWL, no CS.
Monopolistic competition: zero LR profit, excess capacity.
Prisoners' dilemma: dominant strategies lead to a worse joint outcome.
commonMistakes: Setting price where MR = MC on the MR curve instead of on demand.
Saying monopolies charge the highest price possible.
Assuming monopolistic competitors earn long-run profit.
Reading the wrong payoff (each cell lists row player first).
Confusing the socially optimal price (P = MC) with the fair-return price (P = ATC).
examTips: Monopoly FRQs: label MR, D, MC, ATC; mark Q_m, P_m, profit rectangle, CS triangle, DWL triangle.
Game theory FRQs: show the comparison for each player, then name the Nash equilibrium.
For a lump-sum tax on a monopolist, output and price don't change; profit falls.
Know which market structures are allocatively and productively efficient.
guide.cramSheet:
**Monopoly:** MR < D · Q at MR = MC · P from D · P > MC → DWL · elastic portion

**Natural monopoly:** socially optimal P = MC (loss) · fair return P = ATC

**Price discrimination:** power + separation + no resale · perfect: MR = D, no DWL, no CS

**Monopolistic competition:** differentiated · LR tangent to ATC · zero profit · excess capacity · P > MC

**Oligopoly:** interdependent · dominant strategy · Nash = mutual best response · prisoners' dilemma · cartels unstable

vocab.definition: A market with a single seller of a product with no close substitutes.
Anything that prevents new firms from entering a market.
A market where one firm can supply the entire market at a lower ATC than multiple firms.
A regulated price where P = MC, achieving allocative efficiency.
A regulated price where P = ATC, giving zero economic profit.
Charging different customers different prices for the same good based on willingness to pay.
Many firms selling differentiated products with low barriers to entry.
Producing less than the output at minimum ATC, typical of monopolistic competition.
A market with a few interdependent firms and high barriers to entry.
A strategy that gives the highest payoff regardless of the other player's choice.
An outcome where no player can improve by changing strategy alone.
A group of firms that coordinate output and prices to act like a monopoly.

practice.stem: For a single-price monopolist, marginal revenue is less than price because

choices.text: to sell an additional unit, it must lower the price on all units sold

practice.explanation: The price cut on previous units offsets part of the revenue from the extra unit.

practice.stem: In long-run equilibrium, a firm in monopolistic competition

choices.text: earns zero economic profit and produces with excess capacity

practice.explanation: Entry drives demand down to tangency with ATC on its downward-sloping portion.

practice.stem: A Nash equilibrium is an outcome in which

choices.text: both players earn the highest possible joint payoff
each player's strategy is the best response to the other's strategy

practice.explanation: No player can gain by changing strategy unilaterally.

distractors.A: Nash outcomes can be jointly inferior (prisoners' dilemma).

practice.stem: Which is a necessary condition for price discrimination?

choices.text: The firm must be able to prevent resale between customer groups.
The firm must be a price taker.
All customers must have the same willingness to pay.
The product must be undifferentiated with many sellers.

practice.explanation: Otherwise low-price buyers would resell to high-price buyers.

practice.stem: A monopolist faces demand P = 100 − 2Q, so MR = 100 − 4Q. Marginal cost is constant at $20. What are its profit-maximizing quantity and price?

distractors.A: Reads price from MR or MC.

practice.stem: Using the previous monopoly (demand P = 100 − 2Q, MC = $20, monopoly Q = 20, P = $60), what is the deadweight loss?

practice.stimulus:
Payoffs (Firm A, Firm B) in $ millions:

| | B: High price | B: Low price |
|---|---|---|
| A: High price | (10, 10) | (2, 14) |
| A: Low price | (14, 2) | (5, 5) |
practice.explanation: Low is a dominant strategy for both (14 > 10 and 5 > 2), so both choose Low, a prisoners' dilemma.

distractors.A: Jointly best, but each has an incentive to deviate.

practice.stem: A monopolist is producing where demand is inelastic. To increase profit, it should
practice.explanation: In the inelastic range MR < 0, so cutting output raises revenue and lowers cost.

practice.stem: A government regulator sets a natural monopoly's price where P = MC. At that output, ATC is above price. Which outcome follows?

choices.text: The outcome is allocatively efficient, but the firm incurs a loss and may need a subsidy.
Output falls below the unregulated monopoly level.

practice.explanation: With falling ATC, MC lies below ATC, so P = MC < ATC.

practice.stem: Compared with a single-price monopolist, a perfectly price-discriminating monopolist

choices.text: produces less and creates more deadweight loss
produces the allocatively efficient quantity, eliminates deadweight loss, and captures all consumer surplus

practice.explanation: MR equals demand, so it produces until P = MC on the last unit.

practice.stem: A profit-maximizing monopolist faces a lump-sum tax. Compared with before the tax, the monopolist will

choices.text: produce the same quantity at the same price, with lower profit

practice.explanation: A lump-sum tax is a fixed cost; MR and MC are unchanged.

practice.stimulus:
Payoffs (Firm X, Firm Y):

| | Y: Expand | Y: Hold |
|---|---|---|
| X: Expand | (4, 3) | (9, 5) |
| X: Hold | (6, 8) | (7, 2) |

choices.text: X has a dominant strategy; Y does not. The Nash equilibrium is (Expand, Hold).
Neither has a dominant strategy; there are two Nash equilibria: (Expand, Hold) and (Hold, Expand).
Both have dominant strategies to Expand.
The only Nash equilibrium is (Hold, Hold).

practice.explanation: X: if Y Expands, Hold (6 > 4); if Y Holds, Expand (9 > 7), so no dominant strategy. Y: if X Expands, Hold (5 > 3); if X Holds, Expand (8 > 2), so no dominant strategy. Mutual best responses: (Expand, Hold) and (Hold, Expand).

practice.stem: A monopolistically competitive restaurant is earning short-run economic profit. In the long run, which change occurs?

choices.text: The firm's MC shifts down until profit is zero.
The firm becomes a price taker.
New restaurants enter, the firm's demand shifts left and becomes more elastic, and profit falls to zero.

practice.explanation: Entry adds close substitutes, reducing and flattening each firm's demand.

practice.stem: Why are cartel agreements among oligopolists often unstable?

choices.text: Demand is perfectly elastic for cartel products.
Each member can increase its own profit by secretly producing more than its quota at the high cartel price.

practice.explanation: The incentive to cheat mirrors the prisoners' dilemma.

practice.prompt:
Two firms, Xeno and Yarra, each decide simultaneously whether to advertise. Payoffs are profits in millions (Xeno, Yarra); both know the matrix.

| | Yarra: Advertise | Yarra: Don't advertise |
|---|---|---|
| Xeno: Advertise | (8, 6) | (12, 4) |
| Xeno: Don't advertise | (6, 9) | (10, 7) |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Does Xeno have a dominant strategy? Explain using the payoffs.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Is the Nash equilibrium the outcome that maximizes the firms' combined profit? Explain.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suppose the government imposes a $3 million tax on Yarra whenever Yarra advertises. Identify Yarra's dominant strategy, if any, after the tax.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Identify the new Nash equilibrium after the tax.

rubric.description: Yes, Advertise: if Yarra advertises, 8 > 6; if Yarra doesn't, 12 > 10.
No; combined profit is 14 at (Advertise, Advertise) but 17 at (Don't, Don't).
Don't advertise: Yarra's advertise payoffs become 3 and 6; if Xeno advertises, 4 > 3; if Xeno doesn't, 7 > 6.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) Yes. Xeno's dominant strategy is to advertise. If Yarra advertises, Xeno earns 8 by advertising versus 6 by not; if Yarra doesn't advertise, Xeno earns 12 versus 10.

(b) Yarra also has a dominant strategy to advertise (6 > 4 and 9 > 7), so the Nash equilibrium is both firms advertise, with payoffs (8, 6).

(c) No. At the Nash equilibrium, combined profit is 8 + 6 = 14. If neither advertised, combined profit would be 10 + 7 = 17.

(d) After the tax, Yarra's payoffs from advertising fall to 3 (if Xeno advertises) and 6 (if Xeno doesn't). Yarra now earns more by not advertising in both cases (4 > 3 and 7 > 6), so its dominant strategy is to not advertise.

(e) Xeno still advertises (12 > 10 when Yarra doesn't), so the new Nash equilibrium is Xeno advertises and Yarra doesn't advertise, with payoffs (12, 4).
